anchors.fact: Brian Shebairo owned a hot-dog shop in New York and was turning the bubble-tea lounge next door into a bar; he had first planned a rock-and-roll bar (Proper pp. 269–270, F1–F3).
anchors.meaning: Someone with no stake in looking clever, in a scruffy everyday place.

anchors.fact: The phone booth door was Shebairo's idea; he called it "a little Get Smart" (Proper p. 270, F5). The page gives him the idea, not the building.
anchors.meaning: The joke was his, planned into the place, and played straight: a phone booth that is also a door.

anchors.fact: *Get Smart* was a 1960s American TV spoof of spy films (NBC, then CBS, 1965–70), starring Don Adams as Maxwell Smart, whose hero steps into a phone booth and dials a number (Nash 1976; *Cinefex*; FTS highlights, G1–G4).
anchors.meaning: Explains his joke plainly: a grown-up's spy-comedy gag built into a real wall.

anchors.fact: The bar opened in 2007 (Oxford pdf 521; Proper pp. 229, 242), and Oxford's edition (© 2022) still says it is reached through a phone booth at the back of the shop, with a photo (pdf 1854–1855, F7–F10).
anchors.meaning: It lasted: more than a decade later the joke was still the bar's door, working without him there.

anchors.fact: Simonson calls it "arguably the most famous bar entrance in the world" (his "arguably", Proper p. 270, F5).
anchors.meaning: The small joke left a mark far bigger than a prank.

anchors.fact: The Oxford photo: a narrow wooden booth with glass-panelled folding doors in a brick-walled shop, stools at a ledge, a wall phone inside (pdf 1855, F9).
anchors.meaning: What the door looks like, for the image brief: an everyday booth; no sign is visible in the one photo (that is all the page shows).

cocktail.closingLine: Label the bottle before it goes in the fridge. Then plant your next surprise somewhere it's still going once you've left the house.
cocktail.glassware: a plain everyday tumbler (about 300 ml), filled with ice
method: Make the rich syrup: warm 200 g sugar with 100 g water, stirring, until it's clear. Let it cool.

Make the bottle (six drinks): pour 270 ml apple brandy, 120 ml dry vermouth and 30 ml rich syrup into a clean 500 ml bottle. Close it and turn it over a few times. No water and no soda go in the bottle: vermouth in a watered-down cocktail changes within a few hours.
Label the bottle: the drink's name, "apple brandy, strong", and "70 ml over ice, top with soda". Keep it in the fridge. Use it within about a month; it's at its best while the bottle is still full.
To serve, fill a plain tumbler with ice and pour in 70 ml from the bottle.
Top with 110 ml cold soda water (130 ml if your apple brandy is stronger than 50%) and stir once, gently.
Squeeze a strip of lemon peel over the top so its oils fall on the drink, then drop it in.
cocktail.name: The Kind You'd Want

recipe.item: apple brandy, oak-aged (a Calvados, or an American straight apple brandy, not applejack, 40-50%)
recipe.note: from the bottle in the fridge
from the bottle; kept cold and undiluted, it lasts longer

recipe.item: rich syrup (2 parts sugar to 1 part water, by weight)

recipe.note: added in the glass, never in the bottle
squeezed over the top, then dropped in

cocktail.tagline: Your mischief makes grown-ups feel like they're allowed to play.

reading.epigraph: Poured from a bottle in the fridge, like anything else. It isn't anything else.
whoYouAre: Somebody's keys are in the fruit bowl, under the bananas, and you're helping them look, very seriously. This morning every mug in the cupboard was turned to face the wall. They call it trouble, and they keep letting you in anyway.

Nobody spots the rules. Every trick fits one person, and everything can be put right in seconds. The mugs go back. The keys turn up before anyone's late. For every trick people see, there are a few you decided against, because of who'd be on the end of it. What you're afraid of is the trick that lands wrong and becomes somebody's bad day. So you keep them small, and gone by teatime.
You make a house a place where being surprised is safe, and around you, grown-ups still get to play.
yours: In the 2000s, Brian Shebairo owned a rough-and-tumble hot-dog shop on St. Mark's Place in New York, and was turning the bubble-tea lounge next door into a bar. His first plan was a rock-and-roll bar. It became a cocktail bar instead, and the door to it was his idea: a phone booth, at the back of the hot-dog shop. "A little Get Smart," he called it, after the 1960s TV spy spoof whose hero steps into a phone booth and dials a number.

The bar opened in 2007. More than a decade later, that phone booth was still its door, and one writer calls it, with a careful "arguably", the most famous bar entrance in the world. It's the same bar as another of my stories, but that one belongs to someone else.

I like to think that's exactly the joke you'd make, and exactly how you'd make it: played completely straight. No wink, just a phone booth in a hot-dog shop, where a phone booth has every right to be. Nobody gets hurt. The worst that can happen is you open a door and find a bar. But there's one difference from yours. His wasn't put back by teatime. It stayed. And I like to think it went on catching somebody new on a quiet weeknight, years after he first thought of it, without him there to watch it land.

The cocktail I've made for you is built on the same joke. It's a highball: apple brandy, dry vermouth and a spoon of rich syrup, mixed in a bottle that waits, labelled, in the fridge. Whenever someone wants one, they pour a little over ice in a plain tumbler, top it up with cold soda water, then squeeze a lemon peel over it. It looks like any fizzy thing you'd find in a fridge. It tastes like a proper cocktail: dry and bright, apple first, with lemon over the top. Nothing in it is hidden, and the label says what it is. The only trick is that it's there, ready, long after whoever made it has gone out, as a nod to a phone booth that kept being a door.

Keep your rules. They're why people let you in. But make one that stays. Not a trick for this afternoon: a surprise built into something that lasts. A note in the pocket of a coat they won't wear until winter. A line written inside a book you lend. You won't be there when it lands, and that's the point. Months from now someone will find it, grin at nobody, and know exactly who it was.
